Area.evidence_source: Friendship networks did not provide an outlet for them to express their difficulties. The opposite was often true, in that male friends were regarded as unreceptive to emotional communication. Within these narratives it was clear that men did not speak to each other about their emotions. Furthermore, any kind of confessional discourse would likely be rejected by other men. Therefore this kind of engagement was rarely attempted. Communicating psychological difficulties was regarded as 'taboo'.[/page/12/Text/2]loss or disappointment around male friendship was mentioned by two ofthe men as implicated in their suicide attempts.[/page/13/Text/2]Despite the constraints around confiding and intimacy, it was clear that the men wanted to connect to, and have friendships with, other men. Although they found some elements of friendship difficult and avoided emotional expressiveness or confiding, nevertheless, same sex friendship was for them an important affirming site for masculinity (Williams, 1992; Nardi, 2000).[/page/13/Text/2]Male friendships promote and allow expressions of loyalty, trust, and other forms of reciprocal action and support which are important to men. Such relationships affirm important elements of masculinity.
